items.prompt: Sales says customers want to "export their data." What is that statement?
choices: Proof that customers will use an export feature
A full description of the job customers need done
A solution already, not the problem that sits behind it
items.explanation: A request names a mechanism; it does not confirm what job the customer is doing.

items.prompt: Which of these counts as evidence rather than assumption?
choices: A salesperson's hunch about what customers want
Customers clicking a button and answering a question
An executive's strong belief that the idea is a good one
items.explanation: Evidence is behavior or a real signal; hunches and beliefs are assumptions.

items.prompt: In the cook story, what did the cook assume without checking?
choices: That the oven was big enough for the batch
That guests would enjoy the dish
That the party would start on time
items.explanation: She never tested the one belief that mattered: whether guests would like the dish.

items.prompt: How many of the 200 eligible customers used the bulk export in its first month?
items.explanation: Only 2 of 200 used it, which is 1%.

items.prompt: What does "adoption" mean?
choices: How many people actually used it once it existed
How many people were told that it was coming
How much engineering time the whole build took to finish
items.explanation: Adoption is actual use after something is available.

items.prompt: What is the problem with building the full version first?
choices: It makes the feature too small to matter to customers
It guarantees that customers will dislike it
It commits weeks of effort to a guess
items.explanation: If the guess is wrong, all of that effort is spent finding out the hard way.

items.prompt: "I need a hammer" is most like which kind of statement?
choices: A measured behavior from real customers
A finished test of the riskiest assumption behind a product plan
A stated solution; the real job may be hanging a picture
items.explanation: The hammer is a mechanism; a hook or tape might serve the real job better.

items.prompt: Which is a stronger signal about demand?
choices: What people said they might do someday
What people did when given a real chance to act
What a colleague guessed people would prefer
items.explanation: Behavior beats stated preference and secondhand guesses.

items.prompt: Sales reports that customers want to "export their data." Which description of that report is most accurate?
choices: A secondhand claim that names a feature, not evidence of the need
A direct measurement of how customers behave in the product
Proof of demand, since it came from the team nearest buyers
A problem statement, since it says what customers want to do
items.explanation: The report is a useful clue, but it names a mechanism and arrives secondhand, so it is still an assumption.
items.reference:
A request is a guess until behavior confirms it
💬 Stated: what someone says they want
👆 Evidence: what they actually did
📉 Adoption: use once it exists (2 of 200)
Why: a request names a mechanism, so it stays an assumption until real behavior confirms it.
items.learnMore:
A request is not yet the problem

"Customers want to export" names a mechanism, not the job behind it. Effort committed to it is a bet until a cheap test shows what people do.

Common mistake

Treating a secondhand request as proof that the full build is safe.
items.reflection: Think of something you built, bought or agreed to because someone asked for it. What was the job behind the request, and did the thing you chose serve it?

items.prompt: Three different sales reps all repeat that customers want feature X. What does the repetition add?
choices: Enough evidence to begin the full build without running any further test first
More reason to think it is common, but no behavior evidence
Evidence that X is the underlying problem customers actually have
A guarantee that customers will adopt X once it ships to them
items.explanation: Repetition raises how often the request is heard; it still does not show what people do.

items.prompt: What is validation?
choices: Cheaply testing an assumption before building the full thing
Checking that the code passes all of its automated tests
Asking a manager to approve the finished feature
items.explanation: Validation tests a belief about what people want, not the code.

items.prompt: What is a prototype for?
choices: Replacing the real feature for all customers
Proving that the engineers can work faster
Testing a question quickly, not shipping as the product
items.explanation: A prototype is a stand-in built to answer a question.

items.prompt: In this unit, what is an MVP?
choices: A cheaper copy of the final feature with fewer parts
The first version that goes to the whole customer base
The smallest version that tests the riskiest assumption
items.explanation: An MVP is defined by what it tests, not by how little it contains.

items.prompt: The cook serves one portion to one guest before cooking 100. What is that?
choices: A cheap test of the riskiest assumption
A full launch of the new menu
A discount offered to the earliest guests
items.explanation: One portion tests whether guests like the dish at minimal cost.

items.prompt: How does a prototype's effort compare with the real feature's?
choices: Far less effort and time
About the same effort and time
More effort, because it is tested more
items.explanation: A prototype is cheap on purpose.

items.prompt: Which word best matches what an MVP is built to do?
choices: Impress
Scale
Test
items.explanation: The MVP exists to test, not to impress or to scale.

items.prompt: A fake-door button opens a "coming soon" question. What is it?
choices: A production release
A security audit
A validation test
items.explanation: It is a cheap way to see how real customers respond.

items.prompt: When should validation happen relative to the full build?
choices: After the feature has shipped to all of our customers
Only when customers have started to complain loudly
Before committing the weeks of full-build effort
items.explanation: Validation is only cheap and useful before the big commitment.

items.prompt: A team calls its plan an MVP: the same export feature with half the file formats. Which definition does the plan actually fit?
choices: A smaller version of the final feature, not a test of the risk
A prototype built to answer a question about customer need
A validation step costing days rather than weeks of work
A fake-door test that shows demand before any real building
items.explanation: Fewer formats is still a real export built on the same unconfirmed guess, so it is a smaller feature.
items.reference:
Three terms, three jobs
🧪 Validation: cheaply test an assumption
🧰 Prototype: a stand-in built to answer a question
🎯 MVP: the smallest test of the riskiest assumption
Why: each term is about learning before committing, not about shipping something smaller.
items.learnMore:

Common mistake

items.prompt: Which pair of term and meaning is correctly matched?

items.explanation: A prototype exists to answer a question; the other definitions describe building first, labels or announcements.

items.prompt: What comes first in the validate-before-build loop?
choices: A full build of the feature
An assumption about what customers want
A launch announcement sent out to customers
items.explanation: The loop starts with the belief that the test will check.

items.prompt: What does the test step watch?
choices: How many engineers reviewed the code
How long the roadmap meeting lasted
Real behavior, not only stated opinions
items.explanation: Behavior is a stronger signal than what people say.

items.prompt: If the test does not confirm the assumption, what happens next?
choices: Revise it and test again
Build the full feature anyway, as planned
Ignore the result and wait
items.explanation: A negative result redirects the plan.

items.prompt: In the export story, which step did the first team skip?
choices: The cheapest test
Writing any code at all
Telling sales about the plan
items.explanation: They went from assumption straight to a six-week build.

items.prompt: About how long did the cheap button test take to build?
choices: 6 weeks
2 days
1 week
items.explanation: The button and prompt took two days.

items.prompt: When does the loop reach "build the full version"?
choices: As soon as sales makes a request
Once the roadmap has free time
After a cheap test has produced real evidence
items.explanation: Evidence gates the big commitment.

items.prompt: Which is a cheap test for "customers want to export"?
choices: A button that says "coming soon" and asks a question
A complete export tool with every column and file format
A new billing system for exports
items.explanation: The button costs days and records real behavior.

items.prompt: Which is stronger evidence?
choices: A customer clicked and explained what they needed
A customer said "sounds nice" in passing
A colleague repeated what a customer once said to them
items.explanation: Acting and explaining beats a passing remark or a relayed one.

items.prompt: A cheap test contradicts a team's assumption. According to the loop, what is the right next move?
choices: Build the original plan, since the idea seemed reasonable
Revise the assumption and run another cheap test
Ship a smaller version of the plan to be on the safe side
Run the same test again until the result agrees with the plan
items.explanation: The loop's "No" branch is to revise and re-test; a smaller version still bets on the rejected guess.
items.reference:
The validate-before-build loop
1️⃣ Assumption
2️⃣ Cheapest possible test
3️⃣ Observe behavior, not just opinions
4️⃣ Confirmed? Build. Not confirmed? Revise and test again
Why: the full build is reached only after a cheap test has produced real evidence.
items.learnMore:
Cheap test first, full build second

Each pass through the loop is a bet of days, not weeks. A failed pass is a result that redirects the plan, not a setback.

Common mistake

Skipping from assumption straight to a full build.
items.reflection: Recall a decision where you committed first and checked later. What would the cheapest test of it have looked like, and what would it have shown?

items.prompt: Why does the loop watch behavior instead of collecting opinions?
choices: People are never honest when asked a direct question
Opinions always take longer to gather than behavior
What people say and what they do can diverge sharply
Behavior samples are always larger than opinion samples
items.explanation: Stated preference and real action often differ, which is the whole reason to observe action.

items.prompt: Is an MVP just a smaller version of the final feature?
choices: No, it is the smallest test of the riskiest assumption
Yes, it is the final feature with a good deal less in it
Yes, but only when engineers are in a hurry
items.explanation: An MVP is defined by what it tests.

items.prompt: A CSV-only export with three columns is what kind of plan?
choices: A test of the riskiest assumption
A fake-door test
A smaller version of the feature
items.explanation: It is real code that still commits to the same guess.

items.prompt: What might a true MVP for exports build?
choices: A full backend that exports every field
A second export format for later
A button that says "coming soon" and asks a question
items.explanation: It only needs to learn what customers need.

items.prompt: Which has more engineering effort?
choices: A smaller version of the final feature
A test of the riskiest assumption
They have identical effort
items.explanation: A smaller feature is still shippable code.

items.prompt: What does a smaller version of the feature test?
choices: Whether the limited version works
Whether people really want the idea behind the plan
Whether sales understood the customer
items.explanation: It tests the build, not the assumption.

items.prompt: For "an app to print my recipes," what is the riskiest assumption?
choices: That the app has a nice logo
That phones can display recipes
That printing is needed
items.explanation: The person may really need to share recipes, not print them.

items.prompt: If the assumption is wrong, which plan wastes weeks?
choices: Running a cheap test of the assumption
Asking one customer a question
Building a smaller version of the feature
items.explanation: Real code wastes effort when the guess is wrong.

items.prompt: What question does the smallest test answer?
choices: Is the underlying assumption true?
Can we ship this by the end of Friday?
Which colors would suit the new button?
items.explanation: The MVP exists to answer the assumption question.

items.prompt: A team plans to ship "export, but only CSV and only 3 columns." Which statement is accurate?
choices: It still commits real engineering time to an unconfirmed guess
It tests the riskiest assumption at the lowest possible cost to the team
It removes the risk, because the scope is now smaller
It is a prototype, because the feature is incomplete
items.explanation: Real, shippable code on the same guess remains a smaller feature, whatever the scope.
items.reference:
Two plans that are easy to confuse
✂️ Smaller feature: real code, less of it, same unconfirmed guess
🔬 Riskiest-assumption test: cheapest thing that yields a signal
⚠️ A wrong guess costs weeks in the first and days in the second
Why: cutting scope reduces the size of the bet but does not test the assumption behind it.
items.learnMore:
MVP means smallest test, not smallest product

The riskiest assumption sets what the MVP must show. Anything that tests it cheaper than building real code counts, even if it exports nothing at all.

Common mistake

Calling a reduced-scope build an MVP.
items.reflection: Think of a project you scoped down to save time. Did the smaller version actually test the main belief behind it, or only shrink the cost of being wrong?

To share numbers with an accountant
To print their data on paper

choices: A bulk CSV and PDF file export
A new billing page
A shareable read-only link

items.prompt: How long did the shareable link take to build?
choices: 1 week
6 weeks
2 days
items.explanation: It took one week, against six for the export.

items.prompt: What adoption did the shareable link get after one month?
What does "read-only" mean here?
choices: The outsider can edit pages but cannot delete any
The outsider acts as the account owner
The outsider can look but cannot change anything
items.explanation: Read-only means viewing without changing settings or data.

items.prompt: What is a fake-door test?
choices: A door that has been locked on purpose to keep people out
A visible entry point before the real feature exists
A test of a real feature after launch
items.explanation: The door exists before the room does.

items.prompt: Of 200 customers, 40 clicked, 36 of those answered, and 32 of the answers described sharing with an accountant. What share of the answers is that, to the nearest percent?
items.explanation: 32 divided by 36 is about 0.889. The 80% is a share of clickers, 16% a share of all, 20% the click rate.
items.reference:
Reading the fake-door funnel
👥 200 saw the button
🖱️ 40 clicked (20% of 200)
✍️ 36 answered (90% of 40)
🤝 32 wanted sharing (about 89% of 36, 80% of clickers)
Why: each rate must be measured against the right starting group, or the same result sounds very different.
items.learnMore:
Check the denominator

The same 32 customers are 89% of the answers, 80% of the clickers and 16% of everyone. Each number answers a different question.

Common mistake

Quoting a rate without saying what it is a share of.
items.reflection: Recall a statistic you heard recently. What group was it a share of, and would the number have sounded different against another group?

items.prompt: Only 20% clicked. How should a team read that next to the finding that 80% of clickers wanted sharing?
choices: As a flaw that cancels the finding about what the clickers wanted to the team
As proof that 80% of all 200 customers wanted sharing instead
As a separate signal: interest was narrower than assumed, and focused on sharing
As noise to ignore, since only the written answers carry signal
items.explanation: Click rate and clicker intent answer different questions; 80% of 40 is 32, only 16% of 200.

The same 32 customers are 89% of the answers, 80% of the clickers and 16% of everyone. Each number answers a different question.

Common mistake

Quoting a rate without saying what it is a share of.
items.reflection: Recall a statistic you heard recently. What group was it a share of, and would the number have sounded different against another group?

items.prompt: Why can the 1% versus 75% adoption gap not be put down to better engineering in the second build?
choices: It was what customers asked for, confirmed first
The second build used more engineers over a longer period of time
Higher adoption always follows from a shorter build time on the engineering side overall
The first build was released to fewer customers than the second
items.explanation: Both groups were the same 200 customers; the difference was fit with what they wanted.
items.reference:
Reading the fake-door funnel
👥 200 saw the button
🖱️ 40 clicked (20% of 200)
✍️ 36 answered (90% of 40)
🤝 32 wanted sharing (about 89% of 36, 80% of clickers)
Why: each rate must be measured against the right starting group, or the same result sounds very different.

items.prompt: A team runs a test, then builds the original plan anyway. What went wrong?
choices: The test was too cheap to matter
The team tested with too many customers
The result was not allowed to change the plan
items.explanation: Evidence nobody acts on wastes the test.

items.prompt: What does a confirmed assumption tell a team?
choices: That no further tests are ever needed on this feature again
That one assumption is confirmed, not all future ones
That the feature will succeed everywhere
items.explanation: Each new decision brings new assumptions.

items.prompt: Counting clicks with no follow-up question misses what?
choices: Whether the page loaded
Why customers clicked
How many customers exist
items.explanation: The "why" is what redirects a build.

items.prompt: Which of these is a failure mode?
choices: Writing the assumption down first
Using a cheap test as the first step
Treating a secondhand request as evidence
items.explanation: Secondhand requests are assumptions.

items.prompt: A fake-door test confirmed the original assumption. Was it wasted?
choices: Yes, because nothing changed
Yes, because the build is now running late
No, it confirmed real demand cheaply
items.explanation: Cheap confidence is the point of testing.

items.prompt: Why is a "smaller version" test a failure mode?
choices: It costs less than a prototype so it proves less
It commits effort to an unconfirmed guess
It is too slow to finish before the deadline
items.explanation: It is real code on the same guess.

items.prompt: Why must a fake door say "coming soon"?
choices: So the page loads faster
So customers are not misled into thinking it exists
So engineers can skip the follow-up question
items.explanation: Honesty with customers is part of the method.

items.prompt: Validation has value only if the result can do what?
choices: Be shown in a slide deck
Change what gets built
Be repeated every year
items.explanation: A result that cannot change a decision is wasted.

items.prompt: A team's test shows 80% of clickers wanted sharing, yet the team ships the original export "because it is already planned." Which failure mode is this?
choices: Running the test but building the original plan anyway
Treating a secondhand request as evidence of demand
Counting clicks without asking a follow-up question
Treating a confirmed assumption as proof for later decisions
items.explanation: The team gathered evidence and then ignored it, which wastes the test.
items.reference:
How a test can still teach nothing
🗣️ Secondhand request treated as evidence
✂️ Smaller feature passed off as a test
🖱️ Clicks counted with no follow-up question
✅ One confirmed guess treated as all future ones
🙈 Result collected but the plan left unchanged
Why: validation has value only if it is a real test and its result is allowed to change what gets built.
items.learnMore:
Five ways the loop breaks

Each failure keeps the form of validation while dropping its purpose: a real signal that can change a decision.

Common mistake

Running the test and building the original plan anyway.
items.reflection: Recall a time you gathered feedback and then did what you had already planned. What would it have taken for the feedback to change the plan?

items.prompt: Suppose 32 of the 36 answers had said "I want to download a CSV of my raw data." What did the 2-day test achieve?
choices: Nothing, because the original plan was never really in any serious doubt
Real evidence of demand and intent before six weeks were committed
A delay, since the same feature was built in the end
Proof that no customer would ever want sharing instead
items.explanation: A confirming result still replaces a guess with evidence, at a cost of days.

items.prompt: A fake door quietly records clicks but never asks why people clicked. What is lost?
choices: The count of clicks, which the button cannot record
The honesty of the test, since saying "coming soon" is simply false
The reason behind the click
The comparison against what sales originally asked for
items.explanation: A click shows interest, not purpose; the follow-up question revealed that sharing was the real need.

items.prompt: After validating the demand for export, a team skips testing its choice of file format. Which statement is right?
choices: Validated demand already covers every later design decision about it
Formats are too small a choice to be worth any testing
Formats should be tested only after the full release
The format choice is a new assumption needing its own cheap test
items.explanation: Confirming one guess does not confirm the next; new decisions carry new assumptions.
